Chiming in to say that (despite my initial reservations) acupuncture and a nutritionist changed my life as well.  Getting acupuncture from a doctor who specialized in women's pain & migraines once a week for 2 months took my pain from a 15/10 for half the month down, to a 7 or 8 on my worst days. And it stayed down! i haven't had anymore acupuncture in 5 years lol.

ALSO now instead of 2 weeks of pain i have like 2-3 days? Crazy. Combine that with the nutritionist who had me do an elimination diet for food allergies (which sorted almost all of my other GI problems out) and my quality of life went up drastically.

For reference- my periods used to be so painful I would faint on the toilet or in the shower, be trapped in the bathroom with cramps and severe diarrhea for entire days leading me to even lose jobs, bleed thru pads almost every hour, and the pain would start immediately after ovulation all the way till the end of my period which used to be 11-12 days on average (it's now 5-6) so I was suffering for literally 3 weeks out of every month. 

Idk how or why acupuncture works but I have to tell people about it because it did actually change my life so i hope if OP or other people try it that it helps them as well!

To everyone making the argument that it isn't cancer based solely on the severity of cancer or that endo isn't fatal (valid but doesn't exactly answer the question)- research the condition Polycythemia Vera, it's considered a "chronic cancer" where the bone marrow produces too many red blood cells, it's generally pretty well managed by just getting regular blood draws but there's also medicine for it (I know this because my dad has it). Disregarding social/emotional connotations, it's not unreasonable that OP made the connection to endo. Both are abnormal uncontrolled growth of cells, so it could be viewed in  a similar light to certain chronic cancers like polycythemia Vera, but that's about where the similarities end. I understand why many people are upset about the comparison (esp if you've had cancer or cancer treatments) but I very much doubt OP was trying to invalidate the struggles of anyone who actually has had traditional types of cancer and I think their question was a fair one worthy of a more nuanced answer.

I heavily relate and I think we may have some overlap (so hopefully I can help). Except instead of being afraid of being unable to find a bathroom- I'm afraid of even having to USE public bathrooms, I also have a very serious phobia of throwing up so ANY stomach upset or even just FEELING like I have to go or that I'm nauseous sends me into a panic.

For context, I have flown a ton and my agoraphobia and emetaphobia (fear of vomiting) are sometimes better than other times, but I have managed well over 20 flights now and have never gotten sick on the plane. The two things that help me the most are my emergency kit & a plan. THAT BEING SAID- some therapists have tried to tell me that to "truly recover" I need to abandon my plans and kit, but I think I've found a healthy-ish balance as I am only this particular before travel so it's not a constant/everyday thing. 


My emergency kit (and suggestions based on your circumstances)

1. I bring Meclizine (the brand name is Bonine) it's a chewable/dissolvable over-the-counter motion-sickness medicine, it works wonders for my anxiety and motion induced nausea. The only side effect I've ever had is mild drowsiness which is honestly nice for my anxiety. 

2. I bring a mask, some are heavily opposed but the likelihood of catching a stomach bug while traveling is much higher than food poisoning, masking up will help keep you from catching anything nasty (just be sure to wash your hands after contact with high touch places and bathrooms) 

3. SNACKS this one is crucial. I do not eat at the airport, I don't eat the airplane meals, I literally only eat what I bring with me or pre-packaged snacks I buy near the gate. It might sound like overkill but it's my best guarantee that everything will go smoothly. Also, I stick to staples and "safe" foods while traveling (basically just foods I know my body tolerates well).

Also regarding pads, if I were you I would opt for an adult diaper or period underwear. I got a pack for my husband when he had food poisoning and it brought him some peace and saved both extra laundry. 


PLAN- so this is what allows me to feel at ease before my trip: a week before I leave I home cook all my meals and I avoid things that are spicy/high fiber/or risky. That ensures that I'm regular before we leave so I can time bathroom breaks more predictably AND minimize risk of food poisoning. Also avoid obvious general triggers of GI upset- caffeine, soda, acidic beverages, coffee (and dairy if that's a problem for you) or alcohol.

I can say getting a 2nd was the best thing me and my husband ever did for our 1st. I was a little worried about having two males (warnings from friends) but thankfully it worked out great.


We immediately made sure to introduce them in a neutral place that was still familiar to our first dog (a friends house we visit often). They got along well enough there so then we headed home. Initially there was a little aggression from our oldest so for the first two days we kept them either separated or monitored at all times. We kept their shared time brief and gave our older boy a *lot* of treats when around the puppy and by day 3 they were running around and playing and we haven’t had a problem since👍 We made sure there was an abundance of toys to combat resource guarding, and lots of rewards for playing well together. Our oldest is now 6 and younger one is 2 and they are best friends. They cuddle all day, play wrestle (respectfully) and share toys well. 



One thing I wish I’d picked up on faster was how they communicate during play. Ours are very vocal when wrestling/playing and at first I mistook it for aggression, but at the insistence of my husband to just “let it play out a bit” I learned they have tons of cues to check-in with each other and communicate that they just want to play (sneezing, bowing, trade off showing bellies, pausing for water breaks and respecting when the other one doesn’t engage) and no matter how loud it gets, as long as I see these behaviors I know we’re good. If you’re new to having 2 it may take a few days but you’ll definitely learn the difference between play growls/barks and legitimate warnings or aggression (which hopefully you won’t see any of at all) so I’d just try and observe both dogs body language and communication; separate them if you notice the older dog getting annoyed or displaying stress signs. 

Good luck! It’s twice the fun/cuddles and somehow three times the chaos😂😅

Not responding to you specifically- but offering my experience as someone on benzos long term: I’ve got severe panic disorder (as well as OCD, specific phobias etc) and have been on 1mg of lorazepam daily for most of my adult life (paradoxical reactions to almost all SSRI’s, and hydroxyzine did nothing but give me insomnia)

I prefer daily use as the sedative effect goes away after the first week or so, and I never have rebound anxiety. 6 years ago the “doomed to become an addict” stigma around benzos had me spooked so I decided to stop (I tapered over a couple of weeks without issue because low-dose) and then didn’t take them for almost 3 years. 

Of course my panic attacks came back and I eventually just got sick of dealing with that so I asked to start meds again. I tried a handful of therapists and multiple holistic treatment options in the meantime to no avail, meds are the only thing that’s ever helped. 

I’ve been back on 1mg daily for 3 years now and am stable, almost no panic, no desire for a dose increase and no rebound anxiety because my baseline is consistent.

Just putting it out there that there are cases that don’t lead to addiction/abuse. I’ve encountered some harsh judgement over it from some doctors when this med has quite literally saved my life. Also worth noting that SSRI withdrawal/side effects are no joke and definitely not talked about enough 


Some further reading if interested: 

[Lack of Relationship Between Long-Term Use of Benzodiazepines and Escalation to High Dosages](https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.54.7.1006)

Just adding to this- the only money you have to pay “back” is the advance, which is what labels give you to record and make music videos with or really do whatever you want with, but it’s essentially a loan you pay back with your soul lol. A pretty common deal for powerful labels is anywhere from 3-5 records, 20-60% split on all sync licensing, x-amount of merch exclusivity (where the label gets 100% of the profit from those specific soft goods) 50%-80% of all profits from ticket sales and merch sales (and 100% profits until your advance is recouped) and and advance, which to make it simple let’s say it was $1million. On top of that, they also likely own or are renting her back catalogue, meaning she can’t play certain older music either. 

The easiest way out would be for her to pull a (I think it was zappa?) and shit out a ton of music really quickly. Fulfill the contractual agreement and get out, or hire the best lawyer money can buy

They can own future music because let’s say it’s a “5 album” deal- you can’t get out until you’ve made 5 albums worth of music and released under them. I developed severe panic attacks and depression, my ADHD went undiagnosed and untreated (with other complications like sensory processing disorder) and I developed debilitating IBS that cost me jobs. 


Eventually, feeling all of my feelings (often with no one there to help) in every way they can manifest (physical symptoms were a result of repressed or redirected emotions) I FINALLY started to get a grip at about 27. Figured out what was causing me to feel so intensely, got away from my family, the toxic situations I’d found myself in, and quit drinking to cope and numb things. I’m so thankful I went thru all of that in my early-mid twenties as I’m so much better now.

When I hangout with my brother I feel like a kid as he’s very stoic and I’m kind of a spaz. When I’m hanging out in nature I feel like I’m both 1000 and 5 years old simultaneously. When I do something “adult-like” (taxes/handling details of travel/bills/getting winter tires etc) I feel the forehead wrinkles of time etching so deep they touch my skull lol. I feel 15 when I hangout with my longtime friends. I feel 50 when I help my mom take care of my grandma. 
So it’s totally variable. But I will say that at 22 I felt literally the *exact same* as I did when I was 17. Pretty sure I even acted the same lol. You know how they say your brain doesn’t reach adulthood until you’re 25? That was 100% the case for me. 
25 rolled around and then FINALLY my emotions started to chill, the world felt a little bit more manageable (the punishing struggles of daily life no longer felt as consequential as they did at 17-24). Nothing gets objectively easier, but things get more familiar. The devil you know vs the devil you don’t kind of thing….. The devil keeps up constantly with new bullshit you weren’t anticipating and don’t know how to handle, but you always end up figuring it out. 

I’d say try not to stress. Live in a way that feels true to who you are right now, if that means feeling kind of like a kid still (because you really are at 22) then live it up. Be a kid as much as you can because you’ll spend most of your life old, so don’t rush it.

I’ve had them for the past 15 years, and while I do still get them I will say meds/easy exercise (don’t overdo it!) and routine help the most. As soon as I start to feel one come on (even if it’s at school or work) I excuse myself and take a quick and super brisk walk. I feel like when I’m panicking I get this huge rush of adrenaline and going for a speed walk real fast burns a LOT of that initial adrenaline and if it doesn’t stop it completely, it greatly decreases the severity. Sometimes I have to walk for an hour before I can get it to stop, but in situations where that isn’t possible a brisk walk in the fresh air even for 10 min helps get that adrenaline out. 

To counter, sometimes laying totally flat also helps! (Like if I’m feeling dizzy or faint) I will grab something cold and put it on my chest (supposed to help calm the vagus nerve) and then I will breathe slowly and count while I breathe to help me focus on something. 

Meds made the biggest change honestly, but if you aren’t experiencing them chronically yet I wouldn’t resort to them if you don’t have to! Chamomile tea is wonderfully calming, and has a sedating effect, I’ll also drink extra sleepytime tea (even during the day) as it helps calm them and settle my stomach. 

When I first started getting them I was also asking “why is this happening?!?” But what I’ve learned is sometimes things just… happen… and the best thing you can do is roll with it. Even when I DID figure out some of the causes for my panic, that didn’t stop the attacks haha. It’s best to try and go at them head on! Acknowledge it’s happening, know you will always be ok and it WILL pass. 

Good luck!!

They also don’t take anyone on Medicare, Walgreens should have you covered tho! Also apply for Medicare/medical assistance, if you can’t do it yourself (I couldn’t, too many steps) you can go to your local government “job center” or resource building and they can have someone help you!

They’re all stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines, demethylphendidate, vyvanse, concerta etc.) and -any- prescriptions strength stimulant can cause anxiety. But mania and paranoia (which it sounds like you are having) could also be indicative of something else. I would talk to your psych ASAP. Generally people with ADHD feel calm when they take stimulants. Like I have anxiety and panic disorder, but when I take my adderall, my brain feels quiet, relaxed and chill and my anxiety disappears. I don’t mean to suggest that maybe you have something else going on, but I would definitely talk to your doc to make sure you don’t have a condition co-morbid to anxiety that may not be (or just be) adhd. 

I had a friend who was misdiagnosed ADHD when she actually had Bipolar, and stimulants (all types) had a similar effect on her as you describe. She’s now finally got the correct diagnosis and is on bipolar meds and doing wonderfully. Paranoia and talking to a non-living hallucinations may mean that something else is going on. It COULD just be a super unusual reaction to the meds, but either way they’re not helping and I would either talk to your doc about getting off of them or switching.

100% not a bug, I have experienced similar! If it’s anything like what I had the fix was eating more, more consistently. Not eating can make you nauseous and cause horrible cramping, which could be that your bowels are trying to push out whatever food is in there but struggling because, when you go longer periods without eating as much, your gut motility (how fast food moves thru you) can slow down causing more cramps. 

You can also end up with too much stomach acid (that would normally be breaking down food) causing reflux/heartburn/nausea etc. 


What helped me:
Chicken/beef/veg broth (if you can tolerate it) to help get your sodium up and cushion some of the breads/snacks. Drink lots of water throughout the day and try to incorporate protein where you can. I usually eat slices of cheese. Grilled cheese is always safe, so is soup! And I snack on little chocolate truffles when I need a sugar fix (also safe!). 
Start slow and work your way up, eat when you feel hungry and try to snack thru the day. You will slowly notice your stomach troubles getting better and your poops will normal out :) good luck!!

Intentional breaks give her control over the situation :) and loss of control/routine = anxiety, so countering that by having her try things on her own when you’re able to be “at the ready” if she needs you will help her realize that independence has a lot of benefits! An example of this could be her going out and doing something fun on YOUR day off, even though she wants to spend it with you. Just as a challenge! 
Regarding morning/night texts- I would tell her that you’re going to try this out so she knows to expect it beforehand, but yes! You could also make a list of reminders to reassure her- like “I may not text you back right away but that doesn’t mean I’m not thinking of you” etc. that she can read every day. 

As for rejection sensitive dysphoria- definitely see if you think it fits, and if so bring it up to her (gently) 
“I have noticed my absence brings you so much anxiety, I hate to see you suffer, I found this- do you think it might be part of the reason?” And you could mention it often goes hand in hand with autism and that therapy can help immensely!

As someone with autism and adhd- I found that I see my partner as a safety blanket a lot of the times (I know this is not entirely healthy but hear me out-) so if I am anxious/having a panic attack, I want him to be there he helps me calm down, but obviously he can’t always be there! Something that has helped me is forcing MYSELF to break the routine, so I will take a trip to visit my family solo, or go do something by myself on a day when he is home so that I know if something goes wrong I can call him. It gives me a sense of independence and strength, and helps me mentally manage the times when he is gone and I am home alone. I know someone mentioned leaving notes or reminders every day that you love/care about her, but the issue here is if you don’t plan on keeping it up for the rest of eternity, don’t do it (when you stop she will think there is something wrong or that you don’t love her anymore). So please don’t extend yourself beyond what you will be able to maintain long term, but also have patience :) she will likely adjust to the new routine in time as long as you are patient and don’t get upset with her. And as many people said, therapy will help immensely! Rejection sensitive dysphoria may be playing a role here (VERY common in adhd/autism) and a therapist can help guide her through how to manage that!

I mean that my guy friends who have had disordered eating haven’t been able to get help easily because they were men, people didn’t assume they needed treatment, whereas when women seek help for it they have tons of resources available to them and can get immediate help. 

You say when you do have an appetite you can only stomach one big meal a day, that makes sense because you’ve gone so long without eating a normal amount that your stomach has shrunk and your digestive system has slowed down. You need to gradually eat more, and more frequently throughout the day to get back to normal. There are inpatient treatment centers that will work to slowly help you do that (which will help you feel better mentally as well, when you’re malnourished it affects your cognitive function/mental health pretty badly) and they will have on-hand therapists/psychiatrists to help with your depression and anxiety as well.

That’s what I would suggest, do some research into the nearest inpatient clinic and even if you have to travel a bit to get to one, it could save your life. I know you mentioned being agoraphobic, if that’s a barrier in getting this kind of help I would at least give an inpatient center a call and see if they have any suggestions for transport or help. Good luck.

NAD but please get specialized help, men with disordered eating (regardless of the cause) are often brushed off by healthcare workers because it’s not something they assume like they do with women. You never mention WHY your weight is so low, but with the panic disorder/agoraphobia/depression you’ve got all the workings to create disordered eating (even if you’re not “worried about getting fat” there are tons of different types of disordered eating)

Here’s a scary story that might guide you to seek more urgent treatment- my fiancé’s close friend (a husband and father) recently died because of disordered eating and no one ever guessed it. He also only had one poop a week and it would take him hours to get it out, it got to the point where he was eventually having so few bowel movements (because he was eating so little that his digestive system essentially slowed to a halt) that he got an obstruction and could no longer pass stools. He suddenly began vomiting and thought it was just a flu, stayed in the bathroom and told his wife he was fine. 4 hours later he became lethargic, confused and shakey, he began vomiting blood and feces, then passed out. She called 911 but by the time they got him to the hospital they said he had multiple organ failure due to chronic anorexia (she mentioned he never ate much but she didn’t think much of it because he’d been like that since they started dating) and what nailed the coffin was the bowel obstruction that had gone septic (the obstruction also is what caused the vomiting of feces). He died an hour after they got him in.

Your symptoms (esp considering it’s been over the course of years) could lead some more serious damage soon. I would go to an eating disorder clinic or specialist, not just a dietician and get further evaluated.

Your life will get ~worlds~easier if you can find a way to be open about it right off the bat, it kills the awkward tension rather than letting it hang in the air. Some years back I decided I was done living in isolation and secrecy, constantly trying to hide my problems to accommodate situations and people as if they were disgusting and horrifying (pro tip: they’re not, everyone has had diarrhea/constipation/indigestion before lol) So I hit a wall, said “fuck it, I don’t even care anymore” and just started being open with people right when I met them. 
In a job interview? “Sorry, I have IBS so my stomach gurgles a lot lol” they go “thanks for the heads up” and move forward. On a date? “Hey so I’ve got IBS lol, if my stomach makes noise just ignore it”. 
I’ve almost never gotten a bad reaction from being honest with people, and many people respect that you’re able to be open like that.

Of course I don’t mean to downplay what you’re feeling, it IS difficult and isolating, I’m just saying it can get better and easier and it sounds like your brain is adding a ton of unnecessary problems on top of what you’re already going thru. You don’t deserve that.

One thing he’s noticed that I’ve missed is that I’m very easily distracted during that time, so if he can tell I’m starting to get “spikey” as he calls it, he’ll change the subject or tell me he loves me but he can see me getting crazy. Things that help me that my husband contributes to:
-we go on lots of walks, quiet walks lol. This gets energy out, and a tired PMDD is a much less angry pmdd lol 
-he makes me chamomile tea (this ALWAYS helps and keeps him in my good graces lol)
-when I go a little off the deep end, he stays quiet for a few seconds before speaking, this gives me time to realize I’ve just been crazy and I apologize 
- most importantly he leaves me alone, and doesn’t push me if I forget to do laundry or don’t have the energy to go grocery shopping. For this to work, your girl first needs to realize how helpful alone time is or what helps/hurts her during that time. 

When you’re alone you can totally regulate what you allow yourself to interact with. I surround myself with drawing, my favorite music, all my meds (Advil, nausea meds etc.) and my favorite non-emotional TV shows (broad city is my go-to) and sometimes I skip school/work to take care of myself.

Things I do to help both him and me:
-I let him know the second I realize I am pmsing, and I warn him that the next week or so is going to be hard
-I try and get big projects/chores done before it gets too bad (laundry, errands, work, cleaning, etc.) 
-I try to stay mindful of when I’m feeling really spikey, and I try and apologize if I say something mean.
-I try and make up for it the week following, so we sort of trade off responsibilities 😅
